utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Peter McCloskey for the Prosecutor, with Gramsci di Fazio and Phil Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic on behalf of Mr. Blagoje Simic, and today with me is my learned colleague from Houston. Allow him to present himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Peter Murphy. I'm the legal consultant on behalf of Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Attorney Novak Lukic, representing Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Borislav Pisarevic for Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a hearing for the admission of transcript evidence under Rule 92 bis. The transcripts are from two cases: the Celebici case in respect of three witnesses, and the Tadic case in respect of seven witnesses. We will begin with the Prosecution, and we will deal with the transcripts individually. So I'll hear the Prosecution in relation to the first transcript, Marie-Janine Cadic, and then I'll hear responses from the Defence, and we move to the others in order. The submissions should be very brief, because we already have the written submissions. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I recently received a draft report from Robert Donia, our expert and scholar, in the background of the conflict, and in that regard I have noted in my recent review of the testimony of Drs. Greve and Calic that much of the material is cumulative. And since Robert Donia will be here to testify fully, I believe it's appropriate for me to withdraw the transcripts of Dr. Calic and Ms. Greve. For that reason, there's no sense in putting repetitive material in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I've spoken with Defence counsel just before trial and given them an outline. In addition, we've looked more carefully into the background of Mr. Muhamed Vejzagic and feel that he is not an appropriate witness and would withdraw him at this time. And also, as I think we mentioned in our motion, since Mr. Lukac and Mr. Tihic will be witnesses in the case, as I reviewed their testimony, I decided it would be simpler to withdraw their testimony in previous trials and just have them testify about the various points fully so they can also be fully cross-examined by the Defence. And in addition, after reviewing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you withdrawing Lukac and Tihic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In addition, after reviewing the Defence response and carefully reviewing this Court's decision in the Sikirica case and the Trial Chamber I's decision in the Tuta Stela case, especially in regard to the adequacy of cross-examination of various transcripts, it is my view that the cross -- there was no cross-examination of Mr. Doko, so that was inadequate and we do not object to him being called to be cross-examined. And in my view the cross-examinations of Mr. Kranjc and Mr. Selak did not cover the points regarding international armed conflict, and therefore we would not object to the cross-examination of those two witnesses either. And therefore that leaves us only today with the testimonies of Professor Gow, in both the Tadic case and the Celebici case, and my view of that cross-examination indicates that he was questioned point by point, and that was an adequate cross-examination, so I would be objecting to cross-examination of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify something, Mr. McCloskey, you have identified three witnesses in respects of whom you are not objecting to cross-examination, Doko, Kranjc and Selak, but does that mean that you would still like to have the transcript admitted? Because if that is so, then we will have to rule on the admission of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we would like that admitted and -- but due to the simplicity of their witnesses, we shouldn't need any -- I don't -- well, a lengthy direct examination. So I would like those transcripts admitted and counsel could cross-examine on the transcripts and that particular area, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything more to say in respect of the admission of the transcript of Dr. James Gow in both Celebici and Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, besides that I believe he was adequately cross-examined. His material is specific to international armed conflict, and I think it would be a great time-saving device to review his transcripts and not have him brought back to be cross-examined, because he already has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Defence counsel? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I appreciate this very constructive approach from our colleague from the Prosecutor bench. As I well understood, we are going to be able to cross-examine Mr. Lukac, Mr. Tihic, Mr. Doko, Mr. Kranjc and Mr. Selak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, Mr. Kranjc and Mr. Selak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in addition to these three, Mr. Lukac and Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are going to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at page 11 of annex of Prosecutor motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The application is withdrawn in respect of those so that they will be called as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: They will be called as witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. They will be called. They have been on the witness list. They are critical witnesses for the Prosecution and it just seemed not necessary to have their transcripts in in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Doko, Kranjc and Selak might be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, Your Honours, in order to be precise and brief, we have decided, as the Defence counsel here, to argue a certain portion of this issue. Briefly, my colleagues will go through certain important points related to the Rule 92 bis and the spirit of this rule. I would give a very short submission, although I was ready to give an expanded version, but thanks to our colleagues from Prosecution, I will be focused only on the testimony of Dr. Gow. So if it please the Court, I will ask for permission that my colleague will give the additional submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I would wish to address one very short point, which I anticipate may be relevant to each of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accused, but as far as the Prosecution witnesses are concerned, if I've followed what has been said, I think is probably only relevant now to Professor Gow, a witness whose purpose is to testify that an international armed conflict existed, this of course being necessary proof in regard to charges brought under Article 2. Very briefly, Your Honours, my submission is this: That in the state of the law of this Tribunal, as it now stands, including the recent decisions of this Trial Chamber and the Trial Chamber I, the Defence is entitled, as of right, to cross-examine any witness who has to deal with the issue of international armed conflict. Now, Your Honour, the basis of that submission is as follows: Both in this Trial Chamber, in the Sikirica case, and also in the Naletilic case in Trial Chamber I, the assumption, I think, was made that the international armed conflict provision is only, as one court put it, contextual; in other words, that is that it is to be proved only as a prerequisite and is not a critical element of the charge against the accused. And the court will recall that a distinction was made between contextual matters, on the one hand and, on the other hand, matters which are relevant to the accused's conduct or could be described as critical elements. As Trial Chamber I noted, however, Your Honour, in a footnote, paragraph 11 of its opinion, in the Naletilic case, it is now in my submission binding authority deriving from the Appeals Chamber in Celebici that the element of international armed conflict is in fact an essential element of offences falling under Article 2, and not simply contextual. Trial Chamber I sought to distinguish that by referring to the separate opinion of Judges Hunt and Bennouna in that case. However, it seems clear, Your Honour, in my respectful submission, that as far as the principle of stare decisis is concerned, the opinion of the majority in Celebici is binding upon this Trial Chamber and as such we must regard the international armed conflict as an essential element or a critical element of the Article 2 offences. That being so, and of course, in parenthesis, the Celebici Appeals Chamber was considering explicitly the issue of cumulative charging which arises in the present case also because the Prosecution has not yet elected which of the cumulative charges to pursue, and in my submission, Your Honour, it is now the law of this Tribunal, until an Appeals Chamber holds otherwise, that where a witness testifies as to international armed conflict, that witness does so on a matter which is in fact a critical element of the offence, and in those circumstances, we ought to be entitled, as a matter of law, to cross-examine Dr. Gow. Your Honour, that briefly is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, I think there is no gainsaying that the international armed conflict is an essential element of the charge and of the indictment, but the question that arises in relation to Rule 92 bis is whether it goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused. I believe the contention of the Prosecution here is that the international armed conflict element does not go to proof of a matter relating to the acts and conduct of the accused, and as such it is amenable to the Rule 92 bis regime. So as I said, I don't think there is any argument as to the essentiality of the international armed conflict element, but the question is whether that essentiality would prevent, would bar, the operation of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and I don't suggest that it bars the operation of Rule 92 bis in the sense that the Prosecution would not be entitled to introduce transcript from an earlier trial. That, of course, is a separate issue. The issue which I address is simply whether Dr. Gow should in any event be required to appear for cross-examination, whether or not the Prosecution simply offers a transcript of his testimony from the earlier trial or adduces further direct evidence from him in this trial. My submission is that in this one particular case - and I don't say this would extend to all cases in which Rule 92 bis were applied - I merely say that in cases where the international armed conflict is in issue, then the Defence would be entitled, as of right, to cross-examine Dr. Gow in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that even if the cross-examination in the previous trial had been adequate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, even in that case. Although clearly, Your Honour, it would be appropriate for the Trial Chamber, in its general power to control the course of the proceedings, to require Defence counsel to be relevant and not repetitive in the course of their cross-examination. However, in this particular case, we feel that the cross-examination of Dr. Gow in the earlier proceedings was not as adequate as it should have been. Obviously that's a matter which may be disputed, and Mr. McCloskey may take a different view of that. But in my submission, subject to the Court's power to restrain repetitive cross-examination, we would be entitled to cross-examine Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Unless the Court has some questions, that is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very shortly, Your Honours. In our Defence motion under "A," we raise the issue of whether it is proper for the pre-trial Chamber to admit the transcript evidence at this time. As we understand the Rules, Your Honours, a certain distinction exists within the wording of the Rules between "a Chamber," as in Rules, for example, 74, 89, 91, which, as we understand, has a broader sense and refers to any Chamber, and the words "a trial Chamber" or "the Trial Chamber," in Rules, for example, 85, 90, and 92 bis, which in our opinion refers to actually a Trial Chamber which is actually trying the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, would you stop, please. There is a problem with the interpretation into French.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could that be attended to, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would you like me -- would the interpreter require me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us ensure first that we have the interpretation. It's now working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's now working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So perhaps you would be good enough to repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, just for the purposes of repeating: As we understand the Rules, a certain distinction of wording exists between "a Chamber," as in Rules 74, 89, 91, which has, in our understanding, a broader sense and refers to any Chamber, and the words "a Trial Chamber" or "the Trial Chamber," as, for example, in Rules 85, 90, and 92 bis, which in our opinion refers to the Trial Chamber which is actually trying the case. The pre-trial proceedings, on the other hand, are, in our opinion, as per Rule 75 ter, under responsibility of the pre-trial Judge. This is actually just an explanation why we are disputing the Prosecutor's position from its motion that the word "a" in Rule 92 bis means "any." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just briefly, I will be focused on the issue of whether the cross-examination of a witness was dealt adequately in previous cases with regard to the Defence and the situation in the current proceedings. First of all, speaking of the issue of international armed conflict in the Tadic case. It was in, I think, 1996. Now, after five years, we have a completely new situation. Unfortunately, my learned colleagues acting on behalf of Mr. Dusko Tadic at that time were not able to come to inspect the archives of FRY military headquarters and the other sources. They were not able to inspect any significant document or to have any substantial contact with the relevant witnesses from Republika Srpska at that time. Due to this fact, and after carefully analysing all this material provided by the OTP to us, on the page of 248, when Mr. Orie, co-counsel at that time, was in a situation to cross-examine Mr. Gow after the examination-in-chief, which was at least one day and a half, he did this cross-examination for not more than ten minutes. Substantially, nothing occurred, so we think that we should be entitled to cross-examine Dr. Gow, referring to paragraph 4 of the Sikirica decision rendered by this Honourable Trial Chamber. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which says what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which says what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which says that, inter alia, whether the cross-examination of the witness in the other proceedings dealt adequately with the issues relevant to the Defence in the current proceedings. We think that it was not the case in the Tadic case. In addition, my understanding is that based on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal -- I'm referring to the Appeals Chamber decision on the interlocutory appeal in the Tadic case, as well as the appeals judgement in the Tadic case and the first Tadic judgement, as well as the Kordic and the Celebici. Briefly, at one time in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, various types of conflict occurred, and it is necessary for each case to examine the situation in this particular region. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. My understanding of the spirit of Rule 92 bis is the following: I could agree very easily that if we have several cases related to one area, for example, Prijedor, there is no need to cross-examine and to have a repetitive appearance of the witnesses based on the procedural economy. But in our case, in the Samac case, we actually don't have anything in common with the other regions. Maybe - who knows? - further cases against Samac citizens, maybe - some investigations are conducted now - maybe that will be a case that, from our proceedings, in further proceedings related to Samac area, certain portions of the proceedings might be adopted and added. That was my understanding. So briefly, that would be all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I support everything that my learned colleagues have already stated here orally and what our written submissions have been, but I would just like to comment on one submission that my learned colleague from the Prosecution pointed out, that is, portions that should be used per Article 92 bis. In fact, this Article addresses the evidence and is talking about evidence, transcript evidence given by a witness which would be read out into the record. So the Prosecution is pointing out certain portions which are marked with "PE," and they have certain reference numbers attached to them. However, they should be viewed in another context. Our submission is that these attachments which, according to the Prosecutor, have the same probative value as the transcripts should be exempt and should be treated separately. There is a clear procedure how written documents may be used, and that is in Rule 65 ter. The Defence can be shown these documents and we can be asked what our position was in terms of their acceptability. However, I don't know what my learned colleague's position is now. He has just given up trying to introduce some of these transcripts, so I don't know how that affects these other portions that are marked with "PE." But my position is that these cannot be treated in the same way as portions of the transcript, as set out in Rule 92 bis, especially in its section (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any other submissions from the Defence? Mr. McCloskey, in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll try to go one at a time. I've been spoiled in my last trial. I only had to respond to one argument. Regarding the first argument and the distinction between jurisdictional and element of the crime, I think simply my response to that would be: If this was a true distinction and that argument was valid, that would render 92 bis meaningless and it wouldn't be usable in any context. So I would disagree with counsel's view on that point. Regarding the distinction between "a Chamber," "Trial Chamber," "Pre-Trial Chamber," the Prosecution is very happy to have this Chamber decide this issue, and I think that is clear with the spirit of the Rules, and it is unclear to me whether you're a Pre-Trial Chamber, a Trial Chamber, or a Chamber, but clearly I think the spirit of the Rules and the fact that it was listed as "a Chamber" in the Rule gives you the power and the jurisdiction to make this ruling and in fact is what the Trial Chamber I did in the Tuta Stela case. Regarding the adequacy of the cross-examination of Dr. Gow, we have carefully gone over his testimony and have identified 14 points regarding international armed conflict that were specifically questioned during cross-examination, and it is my view that that is an adequate cross-examination, and of course that's for Your Honours to decide. The argument that international armed conflict must apply to a specific region, this is a novel and a new argument by the Defence. It's our understanding that international armed conflict would be a conflict among countries and that there is no additional proof requirement that it must be specifically involved with Bosanski Samac region, that with the countries -- or the entities involved in the conflict, any places inside those entities would involve it in the armed conflict for the purposes of international armed conflict. And regarding the argument about the exhibits, we are asking that the exhibits related to the testimonies that we have asked to come in go along with that testimony. In many cases, the exhibits are discussed in the testimony, and without those exhibits, the context and the relevancy of the testimony would be somewhat in doubt. And we have made a very careful review of all the exhibits that we are asking for, and each one of those exhibits, in our view, has to do with the area of international armed conflict that the witness was testifying to. And I think as Trial Chamber I did, in the Tuta Stela case, those exhibits should go along with the witness’s transcript; otherwise, again, 92 bis would be undercut because we wouldn't be getting the full value of the witness's testimony. Now, of course, if some exhibit was not on point or was more prejudicial than probative or had some other problem, that may be another matter. We didn't see anything like that, and counsel is not arguing anything like that. So I think it makes sense that the exhibits do go along with the witness transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour? Just as a matter of clarification, I was referred to Tadic case where it's clearly stated that for each particular case is a matter of evidence and fact that each specific region should be viewed in light of the nature of the conflict. Of course, it's not the case that Bosanski Samac population, fighting against Croatia, but speaking about the findings and rulings in relevant judgments and jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 16 JUDGE ROBINSON: We will adjourn and resume at twenty minutes to four to give a ruling in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I give the ruling on the various applications. The Prosecution has withdrawn its application for the admission of the following transcripts: Transcripts in respect of: 1, Marie-Janine Cadic; 2, Muhamed Vejzagic; 3, Hanne Sophie Greve; 4, Dragan Lukac; and 5, Sulejman Tihic. In the result, the Chamber need make no ruling in respect of those transcripts. The Prosecutor has indicated that it has no objection to the cross-examination of the following witnesses in respect of whom an application for transcript evidence had been made: 1, Jerko Doko; 2, Ludvik Kranjc; 3, Osman Selak. These transcripts and the relevant exhibits are admitted subject to cross-examination. We are therefore left with the application to admit the transcript of Dr. Gow from the Celebici and Tadic case. Let me deal first with the legal arguments presented by counsel. It was submitted that the Defence was entitled, as a matter of right, to cross-examine any witness whose testimony relates to the issue of an international armed conflict, the reason being that the issue was a critical element of the Prosecution case. However, the criterion for admission under Rule 92 bis is whether the evidence goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused, and this notwithstanding that the evidence may be an essential element of the Prosecution case. As the Prosecutor said in reply, if the Defence argument were valid, Rule 92 bis would virtually be stripped of meaning. It was also submitted that the phrase "a Trial Chamber" in Rule 92 bis meant that this Chamber would not be competent to rule on applications under that Rule since it would not be the Trial Chamber trying the case. The Chamber rejects this argument. The Chamber is satisfied that the term "a Trial Chamber" means any Chamber, including one at the pre-trial stage. The Prosecutor opposed the cross-examination of Dr. Gow on the ground that there was adequate cross-examination at the two trials. The Chamber follows the test that it set out in Sikirica to determine whether a witness, whose evidence was admissible under Rule 92 bis (D), should be recalled for cross-examination, and I read the test from that decision. "The principal criterion for determining whether, pursuant to Rule 92 bis (E), a witness should be required to appear for cross-examination is the overriding obligation of a Chamber to ensure a fair trial under Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute. In that regard, among the matters for consideration are whether the transcript goes to proof of a critical element of the Prosecution's case against the accused, and whether the cross-examination of the witness in the other proceedings dealt adequately with the issues relevant to the Defence in the current proceedings." That's the end of the quotation from Sikirica. Against that background, I turn to Dr. Gow's transcript in Celebici. The Chamber finds that Dr. Gow was extensively cross-examined as to his opinion of the character of the conflict and the relationship between the armed forces of Serbia and those of the Bosnian Serbs by all four Defence counsel in the Celebici case. The Chamber finds that it is proper to admit this transcript, and the transcript is admitted, along with the relevant exhibits, without the witness being called for further cross-examination. I turn to the application in respect of transcript evidence of Dr. Gow from the Tadic case. The Chamber finds that Dr. Gow was cross-examined as to his opinion of the character of the conflict and the relationship between the armed forces of Serbia and those of the Bosnian Serbs by Defence counsel in the Tadic case. This transcript is admitted without recalling the witness for further cross-examination. Along with the transcript, the relevant exhibits are also admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any matter that anybody would like to raise? The Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From the Defence? No. In that event, the proceedings are adjourned.
